paragraphs: The Lasso is widely used for analyzing data with many variables, but correlated predictors can hurt its performance. Preconditioned Lasso methods address this by transforming the predictor matrix and response before applying the standard procedure. The difficulty is deciding whether the transformation actually improves the method, rather than merely benefiting from a different choice of penalty strength.

This paper develops a theoretical framework for making that comparison without first choosing the penalty parameter. That matters because the penalty strongly influences the behavior of both ordinary and preconditioned Lasso. A comparison that avoids fixing it can reveal relationships between the methods that are otherwise entangled with tuning decisions.

The authors apply their framework to three preconditioned variants and identify circumstances in which they outperform the original Lasso. The analysis also exposes vulnerabilities in these methods and offers partial remedies. The contribution is therefore a way to understand both advantages and fragilities; it does not establish that preconditioning always improves Lasso.
neurips-2013-a-comparative-framework-for.tldr: A theoretical framework compares preconditioned Lasso methods without choosing a penalty parameter, identifying advantages and vulnerabilities.

paragraphs: Many theoretical models reduce a synapse to a single number representing its strength. Real synapses contain much richer molecular machinery, raising the question of what that internal complexity contributes to memory. The paper also gives a theoretical motivation: network models with scalar synapses and finitely many distinguishable strengths have sharply limited memory capacity.

The authors instead treat a synapse as a dynamical system with multiple internal molecular states. They develop mathematical theorems connecting the structural organization of these systems to their memory properties. This makes the internal arrangement of a synapse part of the explanation of memory, rather than treating its observable strength as the entire mechanism.

The proofs introduce a framework based on first passage times, which concern how a dynamical system reaches particular states. This framework imposes an order on otherwise complicated internal states and simplifies the connection between structure and function. The stated contribution is a theoretical account of how synaptic organization relates to memory, rather than an experimental identification of a particular molecular implementation.
neurips-2013-a-memory-frontier-for-compl.tldr: The paper develops theorems linking the internal organization of complex synapses to their memory properties.

paragraphs: Standard dropout can train neural networks effectively by randomly setting hidden activities to zero with a fixed probability. This paper makes the dropout mechanism itself trainable. It places a binary belief network over the neural network, allowing a learned probabilistic model to determine which hidden activities are suppressed.

The two networks are trained jointly. The method approximately computes local expectations of the binary dropout variables, obtains derivatives through backpropagation, and updates parameters using stochastic gradient descent. Experiments find that the learned dropout parameters resemble the underlying neural network parameters. The authors interpret this as suggesting that useful dropout regularizes activities according to their magnitude.

On MNIST and NORB, the method achieves lower classification errors than the compared feature learning approaches, including standard dropout, denoising autoencoders, and restricted Boltzmann machines. The reported NORB test error is 5.8%, better than the convolutional results cited in the abstract. These findings support learning how to suppress activities, while the magnitude-based interpretation remains a suggestion drawn from the experiments.
neurips-2013-adaptive-dropout-for-traini.tldr: A jointly trained dropout network learns which activities to suppress and improves classification results on MNIST and NORB.

paragraphs: Tetris exposed a puzzle for approximate dynamic programming: methods centered on approximating value functions performed poorly, while methods directly optimizing policies achieved strong results. A value function describes how promising a situation is, whereas a policy determines what action to take. The authors conjecture that good Tetris policies are easier to represent and learn than their corresponding value functions.

They test that conjecture using classification-based modified policy iteration, or CBMPI. This brings approximate dynamic programming into a policy-search approach rather than relying on the traditional emphasis on searching a value-function space. The experiment asks whether changing what the algorithm learns can overcome the earlier disappointing performance.

CBMPI achieves the best Tetris results reported in the literature considered by the paper on both 10-by-10 and 10-by-20 boards. On the larger board, its results are similar to the cross-entropy method, but it uses about one tenth as many calls to the game's generative model. The findings support the proposed approach empirically; they do not turn the representational conjecture into a general theorem.
neurips-2013-approximate-dynamic-program.tldr: Policy-focused approximate dynamic programming achieves leading reported Tetris results with substantially fewer samples than cross-entropy search on the larger board.

paragraphs: Retrieving a stored pattern from an associative memory depends on how the network's synaptic weights encode that pattern. This paper examines a complication that can be overlooked: those weights are statistically dependent. Just as correlations in neural activity matter when interpreting sensory responses, correlations among synapses matter when reconstructing previously learned memories.

The authors show that activity-dependent learning generally creates these weight correlations. In the retrieval dynamics they analyze, ignoring the correlations produces catastrophically poor recall. They derive optimal recall dynamics that account for dependencies arising from a range of synaptic plasticity rules, connecting the retrieval procedure to the statistical structure created during learning.

The resulting dynamics involve familiar neural circuit features, including forms of feedback inhibition and experimentally observed dendritic nonlinearities. These features therefore receive a functional interpretation: they appear in solutions to the problem of retrieving memories from correlated synapses. The work links learning rules, retrieval behavior, and neural mechanisms through a common theoretical problem, rather than treating each as a separate aspect of memory.
neurips-2013-correlations-strike-back-ag.tldr: Accounting for learning-induced correlations between synapses yields optimal recall dynamics involving familiar neural circuit mechanisms.

paragraphs: Optimization under uncertainty often depends on a probability distribution estimated from observations. This paper allows for uncertainty about that distribution itself. It considers polynomial optimization problems with a collection of candidate probability densities, organized as a ball around a density estimated from data. Because the estimate comes from samples, the uncertainty set is also data-dependent and random.

Polynomial optimization is already difficult because its objectives and constraints can be nonconvex. The authors show that, with polynomial and histogram density estimates, accounting for distributional uncertainty need not make the problem harder. They construct a sequence of tractable semidefinite programming relaxations whose solutions approach the solution of the robust problem.

The paper also supplies finite-sample consistency guarantees for the uncertainty sets and applies the approach to a water network problem. Its contribution connects statistical estimation with robust decision-making and an optimization procedure. The convergence statement concerns a sequence of relaxations; it does not claim that every robust polynomial problem becomes exactly solvable by a single tractable program.
neurips-2013-data-driven-distributionall.tldr: Data-derived uncertainty sets enable robust polynomial optimization through convergent semidefinite relaxations without adding difficulty under the specified density estimates.

paragraphs: Recognizing more object categories usually requires labeled images for more categories, making training data a bottleneck. DeViSE addresses this by combining labeled image examples with semantic information learned from unannotated text. The model uses both visual evidence and knowledge about the meanings of labels when identifying objects.

On the 1,000-class ImageNet recognition challenge, the model matches the state-of-the-art performance described in the paper while making errors that are more reasonable in semantic terms. This means the contribution concerns the character of mistakes as well as overall recognition performance. Information from language helps constrain the model's predictions through relationships between object labels.

The same semantic information enables predictions involving tens of thousands of labels absent from visual training. In these zero-shot settings, semantic knowledge improves predictions by up to 65%, with hit rates reaching 10% across thousands of novel labels. These are reported upper-end results, not uniform gains across every unseen category. The findings show how text can extend the reach of a visual model beyond its labeled image categories.
neurips-2013-devise-a-deep-visual-semant.tldr: DeViSE combines images and text-derived semantics to recognize familiar objects and predict labels unseen during visual training.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms make decisions sequentially and measure performance against a competitor chosen for comparison. This paper extends exponentiated gradient to infinite-dimensional spaces. A central challenge is adapting to the size of the unknown competitor, measured by its L2 norm, without needing that size as an input to the algorithm.

The analysis shows that the algorithm implicitly estimates this norm. Its regret bound depends roughly on the norm times a logarithmic factor and the square root of the number of rounds. This improves the dependence on competitor size over the standard bound available without knowing the norm, which contains a quadratic dependence on that quantity.

To establish the result, the authors develop tools for analyzing regularizers that change over time, using local smoothness. They also prove a lower bound showing that the algorithm is optimal up to a square-root logarithmic factor in the number of rounds for linear and Lipschitz losses. The contribution combines adaptation to an unknown competitor with a guarantee that remains meaningful in infinite-dimensional settings.
neurips-2013-dimension-free-exponentiate.tldr: An infinite-dimensional exponentiated-gradient algorithm adapts to an unknown competitor norm and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Selecting useful predictors can involve dependencies: the relevance of one feature may be related to the relevance of another. This paper proposes a probabilistic model based on the horseshoe prior to learn those relationships. Because exact inference is intractable, the authors use expectation propagation as an approximate way to infer the model.

Learning the feature-selection dependencies can itself overfit. The paper therefore uses data from multiple tasks to support their estimation, with only a few modifications to the model. The shared assumption concerns relationships in feature selection. Different tasks may still use different relevant features and assign them different model coefficients.

This distinction permits information sharing without requiring every task to select the same predictors. Experiments on real and synthetic data show better performance than the multi-task alternatives considered in the paper. They also show that suitable selection dependencies can be learned from training data alone for the problems studied. The evidence supports this more flexible form of sharing in those experiments, while shared selection dependencies remain an assumption of the multi-task model.
neurips-2013-learning-feature-selection-.tldr: A probabilistic model shares feature-selection dependencies across tasks while allowing each task to use different features and coefficients.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference often asks which hidden circumstances could explain an observation. This paper develops algorithms that spend computation in advance so that many later inference queries can be answered rapidly. The central idea is to learn an inverse factorization of a Bayesian network's joint distribution, placing observations at the starting points of the resulting representation.

The algorithms estimate the local conditional distributions needed for that inverse representation. They can then sample backward through the computations that produced an observation, seeking a likely explanation. This turns accumulated training information into a reusable inference mechanism rather than starting each query without that preparation.

The authors show that the estimated inverses converge asymptotically as the number of prior or posterior training samples grows. To use them before convergence, they introduce Inverse MCMC, which employs the learned inverses to propose blocks of variables within a Metropolis-Hastings sampler. The paper explores this sampler across different parameter settings and Bayesian networks, connecting learned approximate inverses to an established sampling procedure.
neurips-2013-learning-stochastic-inverse.tldr: Learned inverse factorizations support reusable Bayesian inference and provide block proposals for a Metropolis-Hastings sampler.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to find a smaller set of stimulus features that retains all information about a system's response. This is useful when a stimulus has many dimensions but only a subspace matters for predicting the response. The proposed nonparametric method generalizes approaches including spike-triggered averages, spike-triggered covariance, and maximally informative dimensions.

Its strategy reverses the usual emphasis. Instead of directly maximizing mutual information between selected features and responses, it reduces dependence between the supposedly uninformative features and everything retained, including the response. The method measures this dependence using integral probability metrics in kernel Hilbert spaces, allowing the required estimates to be computed through kernels.

The authors state that these estimators are easy to calculate and have favorable theoretical convergence properties, supporting extensions to neural populations or spike patterns. They also prove a conditional completeness result: if the discarded features can be made independent of the remaining features and responses, the retained features contain all response information. That independence condition is sufficient for the guarantee, rather than something automatically achieved in every application.
neurips-2013-least-informative-dimension.tldr: A kernel-based method seeks informative stimulus subspaces by making discarded features independent of the retained features and responses.

paragraphs: Streaming principal component analysis must recover a useful low-dimensional subspace while seeing high-dimensional samples sequentially. Memory is a central obstacle: standard methods require storage quadratic in the input dimension. Merely storing a k-dimensional subspace in p dimensions already requires order kp memory, establishing the output-sized storage target considered here.

The paper presents a one-pass algorithm using order kp storage of any kind. Under the spiked covariance model, it recovers the k-dimensional signal using order p log p samples. In that model, the covariance consists of white noise plus a low-dimensional signal component. The result combines small memory with a sample requirement close to linear in dimension.

This addresses a gap between methods with strong sample guarantees but quadratic memory and methods with output-sized memory lacking comparable sample guarantees. The theoretical analysis is specifically for the spiked covariance setting. Simulations also show success on more general data models, providing empirical evidence beyond the setting covered by the proof without extending the theorem to all such models.
neurips-2013-memory-limited-streaming-pc.tldr: A one-pass PCA algorithm combines output-sized memory with near-linear sample complexity under the spiked covariance model.

paragraphs: A large matrix can be approximated by keeping a sampled collection of its nonzero entries. The challenge is choosing sampling probabilities that produce a small spectral-norm error while remaining practical when the whole matrix is unavailable. This paper focuses on matrices with many more columns than rows, such as many observations described by fewer attributes.

The authors give sampling distributions with explicit formulas that require little information about the matrix. Their approach supports nonzero entries arriving in arbitrary streaming order and requires constant computation per incoming nonzero. The resulting sketch is sparse, and its retained values are also highly compressible, addressing storage beyond simply reducing the number of entries.

Under mild assumptions, the distributions are provably competitive with the best offline sampling distribution. That comparison matters because an offline optimum may depend intricately on every matrix entry and may therefore be impossible to compute in a streaming setting, regardless of available computation. The result connects practical streaming constraints with a conditional guarantee against a much more informed sampling choice.
neurips-2013-near-optimal-entrywise-samp.tldr: Simple streaming sampling distributions produce compressible matrix sketches that are conditionally competitive with the optimal offline distribution.

paragraphs: Lifted inference accelerates probabilistic reasoning by exploiting symmetries in relational models. Observed evidence can destroy those symmetries, making conditional probabilities much harder to compute than unconditional ones. Evidence describing binary relations is especially problematic: existing worst-case results classify conditioning on it as a computationally hard counting problem.

This paper identifies Boolean rank as a useful measure of the evidence's structure. It shows that conditioning on binary evidence is efficient when this rank is bounded. The result refines the worst-case picture by distinguishing structured evidence that remains manageable from arbitrary evidence covered by the hardness result.

That characterization also suggests an approximation strategy. Evidence can be approximated using a low-rank Boolean matrix factorization, potentially replacing a difficult conditioning problem with one whose evidence has the tractable structure. The authors investigate this possibility both theoretically and empirically. The contribution is a structural route to efficient conditioning and approximation; it does not remove the general worst-case difficulty of binary evidence.
neurips-2013-on-the-complexity-and-appro.tldr: Bounded Boolean rank makes conditioning on binary evidence efficient and motivates low-rank approximations for lifted inference.

paragraphs: The paper studies which probability distributions restricted Boltzmann machines can represent efficiently. The issue is representational cost: a model may be capable of expressing a distribution in principle while requiring an impractically large representation. The authors recast an RBM's unnormalized log-likelihood as a particular neural network, creating a way to analyze its expressive abilities.

By relating these RBM networks to better-understood network types, they establish an expressive strength: RBM networks efficiently compute any function depending only on the number of ones in the input. Parity is one example. This demonstrates that the model can compactly handle a broad family of functions defined by a global property of the input.

The authors also exhibit a distribution that provably lacks an efficient RBM representation, assuming an exponential upper bound on weight sizes. This conditional impossibility result shows that even a relatively simple distribution can challenge the architecture. Together, the positive and negative results sharpen its expressive boundaries and motivate considering potentially more expressive generative models, including deeper ones.
neurips-2013-on-the-representational-eff.tldr: The paper proves expressive strengths and a weight-bounded limitation of restricted Boltzmann machines, motivating potentially richer generative models.

paragraphs: Optimal neural coding asks how a population's responses should be arranged to represent sensory variables effectively. The theories considered here assume that neural tuning curves adapt to the prior distribution of stimuli: how frequently different stimuli occur. This paper extends ideas previously developed mainly for single stimulus variables to settings with multiple stimulus dimensions.

The authors study a minimal population in which the number of neurons equals the number of stimulus dimensions, described as the diffeomorphic case. For two-dimensional stimuli, they analytically derive optimal tuning curves under different criteria. These include minimizing squared reconstruction error and maximizing mutual information, which express different goals for the population code.

For higher-dimensional stimuli, the paper provides a learning rule for improving the code. The contribution therefore has two levels: explicit optimal solutions in the two-dimensional setting and an improvement procedure in higher dimensions. This distinction matters because a rule that improves a representation is not itself a claim of a closed-form optimum for every dimension. The work broadens the theoretical treatment of coding beyond one-dimensional sensory variables.
neurips-2013-optimal-neural-population-c.tldr: The paper derives optimal two-dimensional neural tuning curves and provides a learning rule to improve higher-dimensional population codes.

paragraphs: When labels are propagated across an undirected graph, active learning asks which node should be labeled next. A common criterion, V-optimality, selects queries to reduce squared regression loss. The paper questions whether this objective is well matched to classification, where the outcome of interest is often whether a predicted label is correct.

The proposed alternative, Sigma-optimality, selects a node to minimize the sum of entries in the predictive covariance matrix. It directly optimizes risk for surveying: estimating the fraction of nodes belonging to one class. Using properties of Gaussian random fields, the authors extend submodularity guarantees to this objective, giving theoretical support to greedy query selection.

The analysis also establishes that these Gaussian random fields satisfy a suppressor-free condition, alongside their inherited conditional independence structure. Experiments on real graphs with synthetic and real data show better classification performance than V-optimality and related methods. The distinction between results matters: surveying provides the directly optimized risk, while the classification advantage is established empirically in the reported experiments.
neurips-2013-optimality-for-active-learn.tldr: Sigma-optimality offers a theoretically supported graph-query criterion that directly targets surveying risk and improves classification in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Unsupervised feature selection seeks a small subset of variables that represents a dataset without relying on labels. This paper improves the efficiency of a classical pivoted QR method for that purpose. Its focus is reducing passes over the data, which makes repeated access to a large dataset a central part of the computational problem.

The revised algorithm tracks multiple candidate features during each pass and skips calculations that can be proved irrelevant to the final selection. Despite these changes, it selects exactly the same features as the classical algorithm and retains its favorable numerical stability. The speedup therefore preserves the original selection behavior rather than introducing a different selection rule.

Experiments on real datasets sometimes show improvements of several orders of magnitude over the classical method. The results appear competitive with recent randomized alternatives in both runtime and number of passes. The paper also recognizes a tradeoff: randomized approaches may select better features, while carrying a small probability of failure. The reported improvements are substantial in some cases, rather than uniformly promised for every dataset.
neurips-2013-pass-efficient-unsupervised.tldr: A modified pivoted QR algorithm reduces data passes while preserving feature choices and numerical stability.

paragraphs: Large neural recordings often contain shared, low-dimensional dynamics extending over time. Discovering those dynamics becomes computationally difficult as more neurons are recorded simultaneously. This paper introduces recurrent linear models to identify such collective processes from spike trains while supporting much larger datasets.

The method generalizes the Kalman-filter-based likelihood calculation for latent linear dynamical systems to incorporate generalized-linear observations. It also relates closely to recurrent neural-network time-series models. On motor-cortical population data, recurrent linear models describe the recordings better than the directly coupled generalized-linear models and latent dynamical models with generalized-linear observations used for comparison.

The authors additionally introduce a cascaded linear model for low-dimensional correlations occurring at the same instant. This model generalizes a low-rank Gaussian approach, factor analysis, and describes the cortical recordings better than the compared Ising and Gaussian models. Both proposed model classes can be fitted exactly and quickly. Their tractability is central to the contribution: the paper connects descriptions of collective neural structure with methods that can scale to very high-dimensional recordings.
neurips-2013-recurrent-linear-models-of-.tldr: Recurrent and cascaded linear models efficiently capture temporal dynamics and instantaneous correlations in large neural recordings.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces rely on extracting useful features from high-dimensional EEG recordings. Spatial filtering is an important step, and Common Spatial Patterns finds filters that emphasize differences in band power between two conditions. This makes it useful for motor imagery, but its estimates can be strongly distorted by a few artifacts or outlying observations.

The paper reformulates Common Spatial Patterns as a divergence maximization problem. Drawing on information geometry, it then uses beta divergence to make the estimation of spatial filters more robust to contaminated data. This approach changes the mathematical criterion used to estimate the filters while retaining the aim of extracting information that distinguishes the conditions.

The authors demonstrate the method on toy data and EEG recordings from 80 subjects. The stated finding is that this divergence-based formulation is useful for robust spatial filtering in the presence of artifacts. Its significance lies in addressing a vulnerable feature-extraction stage: unreliable filters can degrade subsequent classification even when only a few observations are problematic.
neurips-2013-robust-spatial-filtering-wi.tldr: Reformulating Common Spatial Patterns with beta divergence makes EEG spatial-filter estimation more robust to artifacts.

paragraphs: Sparse models encourage representations in which relatively few components are active. This paper introduces a unified framework covering synthesis models, analysis models, and combinations of the two. Rather than choosing the operators independently of their eventual use, it learns them under supervision for a specified task, such as reconstruction or classification.

Training is formulated as bilevel optimization: the operators are adjusted according to how well the resulting sparse model performs on the task. When the operators are constrained to be shift invariant, the framework learns convolutional analysis and synthesis operators. This connects task-specific sparse modeling with a structure suitable for processing translated patterns.

Exact sparse-code solvers can be computationally expensive, so the authors also construct feed-forward neural networks that approximate the learned models at a fraction of that cost. Under shift invariance, this yields a principled route to task-specific convolutional networks. Experiments in music analysis and image processing illustrate the framework. The speed claim concerns approximating the learned models, rather than asserting that the feed-forward networks exactly reproduce their solvers.
neurips-2013-supervised-sparse-analysis-.tldr: A unified supervised sparse-model framework learns task-specific operators and builds efficient neural-network approximations of them.

paragraphs: Planning under uncertainty becomes difficult when both states and actions have multiple factors. Symbolic methods can exploit structure, but earlier work emphasized factored states and value iteration. This paper develops methods that also address factored actions, starting with symbolic policy backups implemented through constraints.

Those backups enable an efficient symbolic version of modified policy iteration, but handling the constraints naively can create its own scaling problems. The main algorithm, Opportunistic Policy Iteration, therefore uses policy constraints only when they reduce the update's space and time complexity. Otherwise, it performs a full Bellman backup, adapting the update procedure separately for each state.

The authors establish convergence for this algorithm, which occupies a middle ground between value iteration and modified policy iteration. They also provide a memory-bounded version that allows a tradeoff between storage and computation time. Experiments show significantly improved scalability over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The contribution is an adaptive way to exploit policy constraints when useful while avoiding their computational burden when they do not simplify an update.
neurips-2013-symbolic-opportunistic-poli.tldr: Opportunistic Policy Iteration selectively applies policy constraints to improve symbolic planning scalability while retaining convergence.

paragraphs: Online learning performance is often measured by regret: the accumulated loss beyond what an expert would have incurred. When the expert set is large and structured, treating all experts identically may be undesirable. One may want especially strong guarantees relative to simple experts while accepting somewhat weaker guarantees relative to more complex ones.

This paper studies which such tradeoffs are achievable under absolute loss. It treats regret against each individual expert as a separate objective, making the allocation of guarantees an explicit multi-objective problem. A Pareto-optimal tradeoff is one where improving the guarantee for one objective cannot be done without worsening another.

The authors characterize both the achievable tradeoffs and the Pareto-optimal boundary, together with strategies that attain the optimal choices. They provide exact results for each finite horizon as well as asymptotic results. This makes the contribution more specific than a single overall regret bound: it describes how an algorithm can distribute its performance guarantees across experts and where the limits of those choices lie.
neurips-2013-the-pareto-regret-frontier-.tldr: The paper characterizes achievable expert-specific regret tradeoffs and optimal strategies under absolute loss.

paragraphs: Dropout trains a neural network while randomly removing units, discouraging feature detectors from relying too closely on one another. This paper develops a general mathematical framework for analyzing that procedure. The framework covers dropout on either units or connections and allows arbitrary dropout probabilities, rather than restricting attention to one standard configuration.

The analysis examines both averaging and regularization in linear and nonlinear networks. For deep networks, three recursive equations characterize the averaging behavior, including an approximation that replaces expectations with normalized weighted geometric means. The authors provide estimates and bounds for these approximations and use simulations to corroborate the theoretical results.

The paper also shows, in simple cases, that dropout performs stochastic gradient descent on an error function with regularization. This gives a concrete connection between random removal during training and a modified optimization objective. Its scope matters: the regularized-objective interpretation is established for those simple cases, while the deeper-network averaging analysis explicitly involves approximations. Together, the results explain distinct mathematical effects of dropout without treating every effect as exact in every network.
neurips-2013-understanding-dropout-c07cb.tldr: A general dropout framework analyzes its averaging approximations and establishes a regularized-optimization interpretation in simple cases.

paragraphs: Image components can move and hide one another, yet many feature-learning models represent position through repeated features and combine components by addition. This paper studies a probabilistic generative model that explicitly encodes position while combining features nonlinearly. The nonlinear combination better matches occlusion, where one component blocks another rather than simply adding its appearance.

The model separates each component into mask and feature parameters. On artificial data containing mutually occluding components, it extracts the components and identifies the occluding elements through its hidden variables. On natural image patches, it learns masks and features corresponding to typical image components, giving a different representation from linear superposition models.

The authors also use reverse correlation to estimate receptive fields associated with hidden units. They find Gabor-like and globular fields, along with fields sensitive to more complex structures. The results show that models combining occlusion and invariance can be trained efficiently on image patches. They offer an alternative model of image encoding in primary visual cortex, rather than establishing that the brain implements this particular generative mechanism.
neurips-2013-what-are-the-invariant-occl.tldr: A generative image model combines explicit position with nonlinear occlusion to learn components and varied receptive-field structures.
